# Natural Dis-tinction, Un-Natural Selection

Natural Dis-tinction, Un-Natural Selection is the Spring/Summer 2009 womenswear ready-to-wear collection by British fashion designer Alexander McQueen. It was presented on 3 October 2008 at Centquatre (Le 104) in Paris and framed around Darwinian evolution and the human impact of industrialization on the natural world . The runway was staged amid antique taxidermy and a rotating projection of the Earth, with an invitation featuring a lenticular portrait of McQueen morphing into a skull designed by Gary James McQueen . The collection drew broad critical coverage from major fashion media and museums, and has been noted for pioneering digitally engineered prints whose placement aligned precisely to garment pattern pieces; pieces from the show have since featured in major museum exhibitions, including the Victoria and Albert Museum’s Savage Beauty and LACMA/NGV’s Mind, Mythos, Muse .

## Background

Natural Dis-tinction, Un-Natural Selection extends McQueen’s longstanding engagement with nature—its forms, mechanics, and symbolism—and situates those interests within a contemporary environmental discourse. McQueen’s collection notes and subsequent curatorial writing anchor the work in reflections on Charles Darwin, the Industrial Revolution, and the destructive potential of human greed, while balancing an avowed refusal “to preach” with a clear ecological concern . Museum scholarship has frequently linked McQueen’s practice to broader historical dialogues between fashion and the natural world; the Museum at FIT, for instance, explicitly references the Spring 2009 show in its treatment of evolution and fashion’s changing attitudes toward nature .

## Development and concept

According to curatorial accounts, the collection was conceived in two sequential parts that juxtaposed an organic, romantic vision of nature with a synthetic, industrial reinterpretation of natural forms . Program notes and reviews framed McQueen’s thinking around Darwin’s theory of natural selection and the “deleterious results of industrialization on the natural world,” with a contemporary emphasis on print and color . 

- The first sequence emphasizes organic shapes, soft colors, and natural fibers, using digitally engineered prints of wood grain and meadow flowers tailored to specific garment pattern pieces . 
- The second sequence hardens the aesthetic: natural motifs are reimagined with a synthetic edge through angular prints of crushed crystal, references to industrial structures (including the Eiffel Tower), and a granite mountain image derived from photographer Dan Holdsworth . 

McQueen’s adoption of digitally engineered prints at a couture level—carefully placing motifs to idealize silhouette and visual effect—was highlighted by museum curators as pioneering and influential in the wider fashion industry .

## Design and content

The design vocabulary spans McQueen’s signature silhouettes and experimental materiality, articulated through the collection’s two-part structure :

- Organic sequence: 
 - Digitally engineered prints of wood grain and flowers integrated with historical simplicity in single-piece dresses . 
 - Silk flowers trapped beneath transparent tulle referencing Victorian specimen jars . 
 - Whitework embroidery and embellishments such as beetle-wing sequins; metallic buttercups finished with acid-yellow enamel . 
 - Tailoring softened via wood-print suiting, with draping and fringing described in contemporary reviews as among the season’s most notable .

- Synthetic/industrial sequence: 
 - Angular, kaleidoscopic prints evoking crushed crystal and architectural structures (e.g., Eiffel Tower), alongside geological imagery (a Dan Holdsworth granite mountain) . 
 - A diamond print morphing into a human skeleton motif . 
 - Short “bell-jar” dresses and bodysuits densely encrusted with jet, gold, and silver Swarovski crystals to produce a sharp silhouette; materials include Lycra and bonded leather, with a palette of black and white punctuated by vivid brights .

The “Bell Jar” dress has drawn particular curatorial attention. With its specimen-jar silhouette, it references Victorian scientific collecting and Darwinian taxonomy, and demonstrates McQueen’s drive to push material limits, rendering the garment “more crystal than textile” through heavy encrustation .

## Runway show and staging

The show took place at Centquatre (Le 104), a large Parisian cultural venue in the 19th arrondissement, on 3 October 2008 . The catwalk was flanked by antique taxidermy—elephant, giraffe, tiger, zebra, polar bear—creating a tableau that underscored the environmental theme . A metal globe at the runway’s end carried projections of the sun, moon, and revolving Earth, visually connecting the set to the collection’s conceptual frame . 

The show’s invitation featured a lenticular image created by Gary James McQueen that transformed Alexander McQueen’s portrait into a skull, emphasizing memento mori and the fragility of life . Contemporary reporting also noted McQueen’s playful closing appearance dressed in a bunny suit, which he used to briefly “shake his tail” before exiting .

## Release and exhibition history

As a Paris Spring/Summer 2009 ready-to-wear presentation, the collection was part of the broader fashion-market cycle and reached retailers in spring 2009. Contemporary commentators observed that, alongside its conceptual framework, the collection offered eased-up tailoring and commercially viable pieces, particularly in the softer first sequence .

Since its debut, Natural Dis-tinction, Un-Natural Selection has figured in prominent museum displays and scholarship:

- Victoria and Albert Museum: elements of the collection—including the Bell Jar dress—were integral to interpretive materials associated with Savage Beauty (London, 2015), and are presented within the museum’s online Museum of Savage Beauty . 
- Los Angeles County Museum of Art / National Gallery of Victoria: the LACMA-curated exhibition Lee Alexander McQueen: Mind, Mythos, Muse (Los Angeles, 2022; restaged at NGV, Melbourne, 2022–23) featured looks and accessories from Spring/Summer 2009 and emphasized the collection’s role in advancing digitally engineered print practice . 
- Museum at FIT: the exhibition Force of Nature (2017) contextualized the collection within a historical narrative connecting fashion and nature, including evolution and environmental themes .

## Reception

Natural Dis-tinction, Un-Natural Selection received coverage from major fashion media and general-interest outlets, with reviewers highlighting both its ecological concept and material innovation.

- Vogue Runway (Sarah Mower) framed the show around Darwinian and environmental concerns, praising the collection’s opening “world untouched by man,” the delicacy and romance of the first half, and the season-defining fringing. The review observed an extended passage of bright, engineered prints—“new on the Paris runway”—and assessed the crystal-encrusted finale as avoiding melodrama. McQueen’s notes were quoted to the effect that he did “not want to preach” about such a serious subject . 
- The Guardian emphasized the set’s “parade of stuffed wild animals” hired from a Paris taxidermist, describing McQueen’s “latest obsession: Charles Darwin,” and situating the show’s theatricality within the designer’s environmental message at Paris Fashion Week . 
- WWD characterized the presentation as a “powerful” show of “unexpected restraint,” calling it “among the most intriguing in a lackluster season,” and drawing attention to its disciplined execution . 
- The New York Times (T Magazine blog, Cathy Horyn) described the collection as “drivingly contemporary,” with a “blitz” of varied prints—animals, wood grains, crushed crystals, skeletons, and mechanical forms like the Eiffel Tower—each look distinct and intense in color and pattern; the closing bunny-suit cameo was noted as part of the runway narrative .

## Legacy and influence

Curators and scholars have credited Natural Dis-tinction, Un-Natural Selection with the widespread adoption of digitally engineered prints in fashion, highlighting the technical achievement of aligning motifs to garment pattern pieces to sculpt silhouette and produce “multidimensional effects” . The collection’s Darwinian/ecological framing has been referenced in museum exhibitions and scholarship addressing fashion’s relationship to nature, evolution, and environmental change . Its design signatures—specimen-jarlike forms, crystalline encrustation, and the dialogue between organic and synthetic aesthetics—have also featured prominently in retrospective interpretations and displays at the V&A and other institutions .

## Title and stylization

Authoritative museum sources consistently present the title of the collection as “Natural Dis-tinction, Un-Natural Selection,” with a hyphen in “Dis-tinction,” a comma after “Dis-tinction,” and capitalization of “Un-Natural” . Variant renderings appear in some media and social posts, but “Natural Dis-tinction, Un-Natural Selection” is the stylization used by the Victoria and Albert Museum and the Los Angeles County Museum of Art .

## Credits

- Designer: Alexander McQueen. 
- Venue: Centquatre (Le 104), Paris; presented 3 October 2008 . 
- Show invitation: lenticular portrait by Gary James McQueen .

## Notes

- Centquatre (Le 104) is a Parisian cultural center located at 5 rue Curial, 75019 Paris, used for performance, exhibitions, and events . 
- Photographic agencies date and caption the show at Paris Fashion Week on 3 October 2008 .

1.title: Encyclopedia of Collections: Natural Dis-tinction, Un-Natural Selection
1.content:
Spring/Summer 2009; Le 104, 5 Rue Curial, Paris; 3 October 2008

McQueen’s Spring/Summer 2009 collection was presented on a catwalk filled with antique taxidermy – including an elephant, giraffe, tiger, zebra and polar bear – in an art space that was formerly a Paris morgue. It was a fitting venue for a collection that was to interrogate the impact of humanity on the environment. Mounted on a plinth at the back of the sloping concrete catwalk stood a metal globe onto which images of a glowing sun, silver moon and the earth rotating on its axis were projected. The show invitation featured a lenticular by Gary James McQueen, the designer’s nephew, in which the image of McQueen’s face morphed into a human skull, hinting at the vulnerability of life.

The primary inspirations behind the collection coalesced around Charles Darwin, the Industrial Revolution and, in particular, the impact of the destructive nature of man. McQueen divided the collection into two sequences to convey his message. The first featured organic shapes, soft colours and natural fibres digitally printed with images of the earth’s natural materials – wood grains and meadow flowers – that were engineered for each garment. These designs placed the natural and the technological in provocative juxtaposition. While dresses cut from a single piece of fabric connoted historical simplicity, silk flowers trapped in tulle referenced Victorian specimen jars. Although decorative touches were predominantly soft – whitework embroidery and beetle-wing sequins – metallic buttercups on mini dresses dripped with acid-yellow enamels and provided a point of contrast.

The second sequence continued to draw inspiration from natural forms – flowers, crystals and minerals – but here they were engineered with a hard edge and enhanced to convey the synthetic qualities associated with modernity and the human touch. Prints were angular and invoked crushed crystal, metallic structures such as the Eiffel Tower and a granite mountain that was borrowed from a Dan Holdsworth triptych. In one design a diamond print morphed into a human skeleton. Dresses shaped like bell-jars and bodysuits encrusted with jet, gold and silver Swarovski crystals conveyed harsh lines in material form. Sharper silhouettes were complemented by a colour palette that incorporated

 black and white as well as vivid pinks and sapphires, and synthetic materials that included Lycra and bonded leather.

Whilst McQueen stated in the collection notes that he was ‘not aiming to preach’, his belief that ‘we’re in danger of killing the planet through greed’ was fundamental.

This dress’s rounded silhouette exaggerates the curve of the female form, with a skirt sculpted over the hips to suggest the shape of a Victorian specimen jar, an oblique reference to the biological specimens amassed by natural scientist Charles Darwin.

The shape formed a key look for McQueen’s Spring/Summer 2009 collection, Natural Dis-tinction, Un-natural Selection. The show interrogated the impact of man on the environment and featured fashion models interspersed with antique taxidermy including polar bears, giraffes, zebras and other creatures, with the rotating earth as a projected backdrop.

More crystal than textile, the dress’s net base is so densely covered with the glittering stones that it all but blinds the viewer with its sparkle. McQueen often pushed a material’s creative potential to the outer limits, in this case Swarovski crystal.

McQueen’s Spring/Summer 2009 collection _Natural Dis-tinction, Un-Natural Selection_ was a pioneering exploration of digital print design that significantly contributed to the widespread (and ongoing) adoption of this technique in the fashion industry. Digitally manipulated images of crystals patterning this pair of dresses exemplify the collection’s themes—and McQueen’s fascination—with the interplay between the natural and the artificial. The designer and his team achieved idealized silhouettes by engineering print placements on fabric in accordance with the shape of garment patterns. The resulting compositions produced artful, multidimensional effects previously unseen in dress.

Paris Fashion Week | Alexander McQueen
======================================

[Women's Fashion](https://archive.nytimes.com/tmagazine.blogs.nytimes.com/category/womens-fashion/) By Jonathan S. Paul October 4, 2008 11:00 am October 4, 2008 11:00 am

![Image 4: alexander mcqueen](https://static01.nyt.com/images/blogs/themoment/posts/mcqueenss0901.jpg)

PARIS — Last night’s Alexander McQueen show finished too late for the critics to file reviews for the morning papers. But somehow before going to bed Cathy Horyn gathered her thoughts and wrote on [her blog](https://archive.nytimes.com/runway.blogs.nytimes.com/2008/10/03/evolutionary-mcqueen/):

“It felt drivingly contemporary, with the emphasis on prints based on animals, wood grains, crushed crystals, skeletons, and mechanical shapes like the Eiffel Tower. You just felt blitzed by the color and pattern, and I had the impression that no two were alike. Amazing work.”

At the show’s close, McQueen appeared in a bunny suit, shook his tail at the audience and walked offstage. Watch it on video after the jump.

[SPRING 2009 READY-TO-WEAR](https://www.vogue.com/fashion-shows/spring-2009-ready-to-wear)

By Lee McQueen

Alexander McQueen, environmentalist? That was the unexpected message that emanated from the mouth of a runway that was backed by a video projection of a revolving Earth, and flanked by a zoo of stuffed animals: an elephant, giraffe, polar bear, lion, and assorted other endangered species. McQueen explained, through program notes, that he had been pondering Charles Darwin, the survival of the fittest, and the deleterious results of industrialization on the natural world.

Strangely, the thought didn't set off one of his angry forays into the destructive side of human psychology. If anything, the beginning of the show—the section that dealt with a world untouched by man—unbuttoned the romanticism and delicacy that is, paradoxically, the strongest side of McQueen's appeal. Though his shapes hardly wavered from his signature frock coats, skinny-leg pants, and hourglass silhouettes, the wood-print tailoring was more fluid and some of the dresses exceptional. Pink or lemon flowers were trapped beneath short, nude netting shifts, and two of the season's most sublime forms of fringing came draped across the body in dégradé gray or swishing in pink filaments from a flapper dress.

McQueen's couture sensibilities are breathtaking in close-up, where the detail of flowers and birds becomes visible in lace underlayers and then echoed in lace ankle-wrappings incorporated in shoes. He also gave himself over to a long passage of bright, multicolored allover prints, engineered to fit around jackets, leggings, and cocoon dresses—new on the Paris runway, but also part of general trend emanating from London's young designers. Even as the show moved into evening and the part that symbolized the negative impact of twenty-first-century evolution, the black crystal-encrusted dresses and bodysuits never quite descended into melodrama. McQueen said he "doesn't want to preach" about such a serious subject. More likely, he wants to sell next Spring, and this collection, with its color, detail, and eased-up tailoring, looks likely to be one of his most commercially viable.

Exotic creatures: McQueen's bid to save planet
==============================================

This article is more than 17 years old

See pictures from the show [here](http://www.guardian.co.uk/lifeandstyle/gallery/2008/oct/04/paris.fashion.week.alexander.mcqueen)

[Jess Cartner-Morley](https://www.theguardian.com/profile/jesscartnermorley) in Paris

Sat 4 Oct 2008 00.01 BST

[Share](mailto:?subject=Exoticcreatures:McQueen'sbidtosaveplanet&body=https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2008/oct/04/catwalk.parisfashionweek?CMP=share_btn_url)

The creatures populating Alexander McQueen's Paris catwalk last night were probably the most exotic, and arguably the most beautiful, ever to appear in a fashion show. One, in particular, set a new gold standard for supermodel height - but then one would expect that of a giraffe.

The parade of stuffed wild animals, hired from a Parisian taxidermist, were there to bring to life McQueen's latest obsession: Charles Darwin, and how the evolution of the species has become warped and twisted through man's power and greed.

"I believe that we're in danger of killing the planet through greed," he says. "Every species is fragile but animals are the underdogs while we are actually bringing about our own extinction - and theirs." This from the man who uses fur and reptile skin in his work.

The clothes themselves ranged from the breathtakingly pretty (an ivory silk dress embroidered with tiny meadow flowers) to the sinister (a frock coat laser-printed with an X-ray of a fox's skull). And as always at McQueen, it was the pieces in the middle - the clothes which hit a perfect balance between pretty and menacing - that stole the show. A cocktail dress with yellow silk primroses caught between two tight layers of poison green mesh was a standout. If you want a dress that is gorgeous enough to break your heart and unnerving enough to send a shiver down your spine, McQueen's your man: he commands this territory like no one else. But for a coherent plan to save the planet? Looks like the search continues.

Fashion & Textile History GalleryMay 30, 2017 - November 18, 2017

![Image 1: Force of Nature May 80 - November 18, 2017](https://www.fitnyc.edu/museum/images/force-banner-1900x755.jpg)

Explore the [online resource](https://sites.fitnyc.edu/depts/museum/force-of-nature/index.html) for additional information about topics covered throughout the exhibition.

![Image 2: lightning bolt puffer jacket on mannequin ](https://www.fitnyc.edu/museum/images/forceofnature-video-still.png)

Force of Nature Exhibition Trailer

Exhibit Details
---------------

Leonardo da Vinci once said that "those who are inspired by a model other than Nature, a mistress above all masters, are laboring in vain." Nature has inspired both art and fashion for hundreds of years. Fashion designers often reference the natural world — its ora and fauna, geology, and physical processes — to create wildly imaginative designs. As Alexander McQueen said, "I have always loved the mechanics of nature, and to a greater or lesser extent my work is always informed by that."

![Image 3: Alexander McQueen, dress, Platos Atlantis collection, Spring 2010, England, museum purchase. 2010.77.1](https://www.fitnyc.edu/museum/images/force-of-nature-2010.77.1.jpg)

Alexander McQueen, dress, _Plato’s Atlantis_ collection, Spring 2010, England, museum purchase, 2010.77.1

![Image 4: Alexander McQueen, Irere collection, Spring 2003, England, Museum Purchase. 2016.15.1](https://www.fitnyc.edu/museum/images/force-of-nature-2016.15.1.jpg)

Alexander McQueen, Irere collection, Spring 2003, England, museum purchase, 2016.15.1

![Image 5: Rick Owens, ensemble, Mastodon collection, Fall 2016, USA, Gift of Rick Owens Studio. 2016.92.1](https://www.fitnyc.edu/museum/images/force-of-nature-2016.92.1.jpg)

Rick Owens, ensemble, _Mastodon_ collection, Fall 2016, USA, gift of Rick Owens Studio, 2016.92.1

_**Force of Nature**_ examined the complex relationship between fashion and the natural world. The exhibition revealed how nature has historically influenced fashion, and how fashion can serve as an indicator of society's relationship with the natural world. In eighteenth century Europe, for example, nature became an object of renewed fascination as a result of overseas exploration. This fascination found expression in garments that featured depictions of exotic plants and animals.

Spanning the eighteenth century to the present, the exhibition was organized into ten sections, each focusing on a facet of fashion's connection to nature. Garments, textiles, and accessories, exclusively from the collection of The Museum at FIT, illustrated how principles in the natural sciences, such as the dynamics of sexual attraction, have informed fashion design. Elaborately feathered women's hats, for example, showed how the plumage male birds use for sexual display has been appropriated to emphasize female beauty.

Naturalist Alexander von Humboldt (1769- 1859), often considered the father of ecology, characterized the vast diversity of nature as an interconnected global force. He also believed that imagination was essential to experiencing and understanding nature. Therefore, _**Force of Nature**_ began with a series of garments that demonstrate this diversity and the creativity it inspires. Included were a mesmerizing "water" dress by Iris van Herpen that appeared to splash away from the body and an ensemble by Rick Owens that was inspired by the mighty, prehistoric mastodon.

![Image 6: Charles James, Tree evening dress and Petal stole, 1955, USA, Museum purchase. P87.31.11](https://www.fitnyc.edu/museum/images/force-of-nature-P87.31.11-600x900.jpg)

Charles James, _Tree_ evening dress and Petal stole, 1955, USA, museum purchase, P87.31.11

![Image 7: Pierre Hardy, shoes, Summer 2015, France, Gift of Pierre Hardy. 2016.18.1](https://www.fitnyc.edu/museum/images/force-of-nature-2016.18.1-600x900.jpg)

Pierre Hardy, shoes, Summer 2015, France, gift of Pierre Hardy, 2016.18.1

![Image 8: Alexander McQueen, evening dress, Pantheon as Lecum collection, Fall 2004, England, Museum purchase. 2016.104.1](https://www.fitnyc.edu/museum/images/force-of-nature2016.104.1-600x900.jpg)

Alexander McQueen, evening dress, _Pantheon as Lecum_ collection, Fall 2004, England, museum purchase, 2016.104.1

During the Enlightenment, as naturalists classified newly identified plant species, exotic botanic gardens flourished throughout Europe. These gardens inspired the work of textile designers, who began to depict flowers from around the world. The sexuality of plants and the symbolism of flowers such as roses and orchids have also been explored through dress. An evening gown by Charles James with a petal-like stole bestows upon its wearer a sensual elegance by transforming her into a flower. A pair of shoes by Pierre Hardy challenged traditional representations of flowers by rendering realistic images of lilies in saccharine, artificial colors.

The bold patterns of animal skins have been appropriated by fashion designers for their strong visual impact and erotic appeal. However, these patterns are  
often employed in a manner that contradicts their evolved purpose in the natural world. The striking patterns that serve to camouflage animals in the wild are often used in fashion as a way to stand out. The undeniable beauty of birds and the phenomenon of metamorphosis, the most radical form of change in nature, have also fueled the imagination of many fashion designers.

Nature was the subject of intense study during the nineteenth century, with everything from ocean life to microorganisms under examination. This led to the appropriation of natural objects as a form of adornment. Scientist and artist Ernst Haeckel illustrated his discoveries using the microscope in _Art Forms in Nature_ (1899–1904), a book that influenced artists and designers. Nature's geometric shapes and forms have continued to inspire designers such as Christian Dior and more recently the design trio ThreeASFOUR.

![Image 9: Yves Saint Laurent Rive Gauche, suit, circa 1972, France, Gift of John Karl. 88.170.1](https://www.fitnyc.edu/museum/images/force-of-nature-88.170.1-600x900.jpg)

Yves Saint Laurent Rive Gauche, suit, circa 1972, France, gift of John Karl, 88.170.1

![Image 10: Mme. Pauline, hat, circa 1955, USA, Gift of Mrs. Otto Grun. 77.146.2](https://www.fitnyc.edu/museum/images/force-of-nature-77.146.2-600x900.jpg)

Mme. Pauline, hat, circa 1955, USA, gift of Mrs. Otto Grun, 77.146.2

In 1863, Charles Baudelaire drew comparisons between fashion and the natural world, describing changes in fashion to be "as elaborately articulated as they are in the animal kingdom." In an 1872 essay, Charles Darwin's son George Darwin directly compared changes in dress to evolution by natural selection. Few principles of modern scientific thought have had as wide an impact as the theory of evolution, and fashion designers, in turn, have addressed evolution in their collections. Alexander McQueen's spring 2009 collection _Natural Dis-Tinction_, _Un-Natural Selection_ contemplated the notion of survival of the fittest, in addition to the "deleterious results of industrialization on the natural world."

![Image 11: Dolce & Gabbana, evening dress, Spring 1998, Italy, Gift of Dolce & Gabbana. 98.45.1](https://www.fitnyc.edu/museum/images/force-of-nature-98.45.1-600x900.jpg)

Dolce & Gabbana, evening dress, Spring 1998, Italy, gift of Dolce & Gabbana, 98.45.1

![Image 12: Alexander McQueen, dress, Horn of Plenty collection, Fall 2009, England, museum purchase. 2016.63.1](https://www.fitnyc.edu/museum/images/force-of-nature-2016.63.1-600x900.jpg)

Alexander McQueen, dress, _Horn of Plenty_ collection, Fall 2009, England, museum purchase, 2016.63.1

![Image 13: (R) Saks Fifth Avenue, cocktail dress, Fall 1953, USA, Gift of Sophie Gimbel. 75.69.3. (L) Evening coat, circa 1920, France, Gift of John J. Sasek. 81.88.1](https://www.fitnyc.edu/museum/images/force-of-nature-75.69.3-600x900.jpg)

(L) Saks Fifth Avenue, cocktail dress, Fall 1953, USA, gift of Sophie Gimbel, 75.69.3. (R) Evening coat, circa 1920, France, gift of John J. Sasek, 81.88.1

Discoveries relating to celestial bodies, the greater universe, and the physical forces that created them have also led to extraordinary designs. Electric force was conveyed in an ensemble by Arzu Kaprol that featured an image of lightning and conveyed a sense of strength and power.

The natural world has influenced fashion in positive ways, but fashion's impact on the environment has been largely detrimental. However, this relationship is changing, with many designers engaging in more sustainable practices. This shift indicates a new attitude toward nature, from one of dominion to participation. Science and technology play key roles in transforming this relationship, as evidenced by designer interest in biomimicry (employing design principles that imitate nature’s processes) and biomaterials that are grown using biological organisms. _**Force of Nature**_ closes with an examination of this emerging dynamic, encouraging a vital discussion about future directions in fashion.

![Image 14: Valentino Couture, coat, 1974, Italy, Gift of Mary Russell. 96.84.1](https://www.fitnyc.edu/museum/images/force-of-nature-96.84.1-600x900.jpg)

Valentino Couture, coat, 1974, Italy, gift of Mary Russell, 96.84.1

![Image 15: John Paul Gaultier, top and skirt, 1988 and 1987, France, Museum Purchase. P88.76.2 & P87.47.1](https://www.fitnyc.edu/museum/images/force-of-nature-P88.76.2-600x900.jpg)

Jean Paul Gaultier, top and skirt, 1988 and 1987, France, museum purchase, P88.76.2 and P87.47.1

_**Force of Nature**_ was organized by Melissa Marra-Alvarez, associate curator of Education and Public Programs, The Museum at FIT.

**_Force of Nature_** was made possible by the support of the Couture Council of the Museum at FIT.

Special thanks to the **_Force of Nature_** advisory committee for its ongoing support. Advisory committee members included:**Javier Alvarez**, Animal Forensics Assistant, ASPCA (former Avian Collections Manager, Staten Island Zoo)  
**Daniel Grushkin**, Program director of the Biodesign Challenge and co-founder of Genspace  
**Sarah Hezel**, Director, Interpretation & Graphic Design, Wildlife Conservation Society  
**Suzanne Lee**, Chief Creative Officer, Modern Meadow  
**Eleanor J. Sterling (PhD)**, Chief Conservation Scientist, Center for Biodiversity & Conservation, AMNH  
**Alexandra Wright (PhD)**, Assistant Professor of Ecology at Cal State LA (former Asst Professor of Biology at FIT)

Many thanks to MFIT staff who assisted with this exhibition and related web materials. Thank you also to interns Bethany Gingrich and Nelli Ayvazyan.
